paragraphs: Shūkai addresses a practical challenge for reinforcement learning in fighting games: an agent needs to remain a useful opponent during repeated interaction with people. Strong play alone does not capture that goal. The paper presents a system deployed in Naruto Mobile that combines learning competence, generalization across characters, and behavior shaped around human expectations.

The system quantifies game states to improve generalization and introduces Heterogeneous League Training, or HELT. This training approach aims to balance playing ability, transfer across situations, and training efficiency. The authors also design specific rewards to guide the agent toward behavior that people expect from a training partner, making player interaction part of the learning objective.

The reported agent maintains consistent competence across all characters despite training on only 13% of them. HELT also improves sample efficiency by 22%. These findings support the system’s practical value as a training partner and show how deployment-oriented agent design can address more than competitive strength.
icml-2024-advancing-drl-agents-in-commer.tldr: Shūkai combines league training and behavior-specific rewards to deliver a deployed fighting-game training partner that generalizes across characters.

paragraphs: Language models retain key-value caches during inference, but these stored representations can consume substantial memory. Removing selected entries reduces that burden, yet also changes the model’s output. The paper emphasizes that choosing low-attention tokens for removal does not eliminate this disturbance, and that stronger compression can make the resulting performance degradation more severe.

Cache Merging, or CaM, changes what happens to information scheduled for removal. It adaptively folds the corresponding caches into entries that remain. A sampling strategy uses the prominence of attention scores at discarded locations to guide this process. The aim is to retain important token information without continuing to store a separate cache entry for every relevant token.

Experiments with LLaMA, OPT, and GPT-NeoX across several benchmarks support CaM’s ability to improve memory-efficient inference. The contribution is a way to soften the information loss caused by cache eviction. Its reported benefit concerns preserving model performance while reducing cache storage, rather than guaranteeing that compressed and original outputs are identical.
icml-2024-cam-cache-merging-for-memory-e.tldr: CaM merges information from discarded key-value caches into retained entries to improve language-model performance under memory compression.

paragraphs: Representation learning often emphasizes separating classes, but regression asks a different question: how should features reflect an ordered, continuous target? This paper studies the topology of regression representations, meaning the structural relationships within their feature spaces. It uses the Information Bottleneck principle to connect those relationships with the quality of learned representations.

The authors establish two connections. First, lower intrinsic feature dimension implies reduced representation complexity, measured by the conditional entropy of features given the target. That complexity provides an upper bound on generalization error. Second, their analysis suggests that a feature space with topology resembling the target space better fits the Information Bottleneck principle.

These connections motivate PH-Reg, a regression-specific regularizer that encourages the feature space to match the target space in both intrinsic dimension and topology. Experiments on synthetic and real-world regression tasks demonstrate benefits. The approach makes representation structure part of the training objective, with theoretical motivation tied to complexity and target alignment rather than class separation.
icml-2024-deep-regression-representation.tldr: PH-Reg improves regression representations by encouraging their dimension and topology to match the target space.

paragraphs: Online learning must update decisions as data arrives, but older observations can become less useful when conditions change. This paper studies that problem in adversarial, nonstationary environments. It revisits discounted regret in online convex optimization, giving formal expression to the idea that a learner should gradually reduce the influence of its history.

The proposed algorithm uses Follow-the-Regularized-Leader, or FTRL, and adapts to the particular learning instance. The authors establish instance-optimal behavior and improve on the non-adaptive baseline of gradient descent with a constant learning rate. This connects forgetting to regularization: the theory of adaptive online optimization can guide the design of regularizers for lifelong learning.

The paper also applies the approach to online conformal prediction, where a system repeatedly produces uncertainty sets for a black-box model. The FTRL structure simplifies the conventional gradient-descent-based analysis and yields guarantees that depend on the instance. Together, these results connect adaptive learning rules with both changing environments and sequential uncertainty prediction.
icml-2024-discounted-adaptive-online-lea.tldr: An adaptive FTRL algorithm uses discounted regret to guide forgetting and regularization, with additional guarantees for online uncertainty prediction.

paragraphs: Text-guided diffusion models can struggle when a prompt describes several objects or attributes. Distinct concepts may merge or overlap in the generated image, a problem called concept bleeding. This paper investigates that failure and identifies cross-attention spreading outside the intended object region as its primary source, including attention extending into backgrounds or unrelated objects.

The proposed Entity Localization and Anchoring method, or ELA, acts during inference. It first identifies the image region associated with each entity, then uses a tailored loss to keep that entity focused within its designated area. This connects a spatial diagnosis of the problem with a spatial correction applied while generating the image.

ELA requires no training, whereas the prior approach described in the abstract relies on training an auxiliary object detector to produce constrained regions. Extensive experiments show stronger ability to generate multiple objects as requested in text. The findings support inference-time attention control as a way to ease concept bleeding and improve correspondence between prompts and images.
icml-2024-easing-concept-bleeding-in-dif.tldr: ELA reduces concept bleeding by locating entities and anchoring their attention to intended image regions during inference.

paragraphs: Standard distributionally robust optimization minimizes the largest risk across several distributions. Minimax excess risk optimization instead considers how far performance falls short of the best achievable risk for each distribution. This helps suppress the influence of differing noise levels, but makes optimization harder because those distribution-specific minimum risks must also be accounted for.

The paper develops efficient stochastic methods that directly address this objective. It estimates each distribution’s minimum risk using stochastic convex optimization, then treats the overall problem as stochastic convex-concave optimization. Estimation errors introduce biased gradients, so existing guarantees for that optimization framework do not apply directly. The central analysis shows that this bias remains controlled.

With the bias controlled, the authors obtain a nearly optimal convergence rate for minimax excess risk optimization. They also study unequal sample availability across distributions and derive distribution-dependent rates. These results make the formulation more tractable while explicitly accounting for the uncertainty introduced by estimating the reference risks.
icml-2024-efficient-stochastic-approxima.tldr: The paper makes minimax excess risk optimization efficient by controlling the gradient bias caused by estimating each distribution’s minimum risk.

paragraphs: Some language-model reasoning methods generate several possible intermediate steps and ask a model to evaluate which ones should guide the next stage. That evaluation can be noisy and unreliable, causing the search to follow unpromising paths. This paper focuses on improving the selection process rather than simply generating more candidate reasoning steps.

The proposed method asks the model to compare two candidates directly instead of assigning each an independent score. In every round, intermediate thoughts are paired randomly, and the model chooses the more promising member of each pair. Repeating this process identifies promising candidates through relative judgments, changing the feedback the search asks the evaluator to provide.

Pairwise comparisons can still be noisy, so the authors develop two variants using ideas from ensemble learning and dueling bandits. Experiments on three real-world tasks demonstrate the algorithm’s effectiveness and support the rationale for pairwise evaluation. The findings suggest that the format of evaluation is an important component of language-model-guided reasoning search.
icml-2024-generating-chain-of-thoughts-w.tldr: Pairwise comparisons help a language model select promising intermediate reasoning steps despite noisy evaluation feedback.

paragraphs: Equivariant graph neural networks model geometric systems while respecting their spatial symmetries. Large graphs create an efficiency problem, and keeping only sparse local connections can hurt performance. FastEGNN addresses this tension by using a small ordered collection of virtual nodes to approximate the much larger unordered collection of real nodes.

The model gives different virtual nodes distinct message-passing and aggregation behavior, encouraging them to represent different information. It also minimizes Maximum Mean Discrepancy between virtual and real coordinates to encourage the virtual nodes to spread across the system. The architecture preserves the required E(3) symmetries, covering translations, rotations, and reflections, and has a qualified universal expressivity guarantee.

Experiments cover N-body systems with 100 nodes, proteins with 800, and water systems with 8,000. FastEGNN achieves a promising accuracy-efficiency balance and exceeds EGNN’s accuracy on proteins and water even after dropping all edges between real nodes. These results support virtual nodes as a compact way to retain useful global geometric information.
icml-2024-improving-equivariant-graph-ne.tldr: FastEGNN uses distinct, spatially distributed virtual nodes to improve the accuracy-efficiency balance of equivariant learning on large geometric graphs.

paragraphs: This paper treats a multi-task benchmark as an election: models are candidates and tasks are voters. It distinguishes cardinal systems, which combine numerical scores, from ordinal systems, which combine task-specific rankings. Applying Arrow’s impossibility theorem to ordinal benchmarks exposes limitations in ranking aggregation, particularly sensitivity to including otherwise irrelevant models.

The authors introduce measures for diversity and sensitivity. Diversity captures how much tasks disagree about model rankings; sensitivity measures how irrelevant changes to tasks affect the benchmark. Because computing these measures exactly is challenging, they develop efficient approximation algorithms. This makes the conceptual connection to voting systems usable for examining existing benchmarks.

Experiments on seven cardinal and eleven ordinal benchmarks reveal a strong trade-off: more diverse benchmarks tend to be more sensitive to trivial changes. The authors also find substantial instability in existing aggregate rankings. The theoretical result concerns ordinal aggregation, while the broader empirical evidence shows how diversity and ranking stability can pull against each other in practice.
icml-2024-inherent-trade-offs-between-di.tldr: A social-choice analysis and benchmark experiments reveal a trade-off between task diversity and the stability of aggregate model rankings.

paragraphs: Autoregressive and masked self-supervised learning both train models by predicting content, but they organize prediction differently. This paper develops theoretical frameworks to compare how those choices affect classification and generation. Its central question is why an objective that produces useful representations for one task may be less suited to another.

For classification, the analysis links masked learning’s flexible target positions to more connections between samples than autoregressive learning’s fixed target positions provide. Those connections yield better clustering. For generation, masked learning faces a mismatch between variable test-sample lengths and fixed lengths of unmasked training text. Autoregressive learning accommodates flexible conditioning lengths, avoiding that particular mismatch.

The authors use these findings to design diversity-enhanced autoregressive objectives and variable-length masked objectives. They report substantial improvements in autoregressive classification performance and masked generation performance. The contribution connects specific properties of pretraining objectives to downstream strengths, then modifies those properties to address the weaknesses identified by the theoretical comparison.
icml-2024-look-ahead-or-look-around-a-th.tldr: The paper explains differing classification and generation strengths of autoregressive and masked pretraining and designs objectives that improve their weaker tasks.

paragraphs: Quantizing a trained language model reduces numerical precision but introduces errors that can damage its capabilities. LQER combines quantization with a low-rank approximation of the resulting error. The goal is to recover capability while keeping the benefits of reduced precision, using an error structure that can be represented compactly.

The method uses a scale matrix derived from activations to reshape the singular-value distribution of quantization error. This makes the error more suitable for low-rank approximation. It supports W4A8 quantization, using four-bit weights and eight-bit activations, without knowledge distillation, grid search, or gradient-based iterative optimization. Its computation also avoids specialized Scatter and Gather operations for collecting high-precision weights from irregular memory locations.

Across the reported language models and six downstream tasks, LQER achieves nearly lossless performance. The authors report using 1.36 times fewer hardware resources than the leading comparison method. The findings connect numerical error reconstruction with hardware-friendly computation, showing that compression quality and implementation structure can be addressed together.
icml-2024-lqer-low-rank-quantization-err.tldr: LQER reshapes and approximates quantization error to achieve nearly lossless four-bit-weight language models with reduced hardware requirements.

paragraphs: Machine learning for linear and mixed-integer linear programming needs suitable training problems, but real instances can be scarce. Synthetic instances must resemble the original data while preserving properties needed for reliable labels. In particular, feasibility concerns whether a valid solution exists, and boundedness prevents the objective from improving without a finite limit.

MILP-FBGen is a diffusion-based framework for generating these optimization instances. It combines a structure-preserving generation module with sampling constrained by feasibility and boundedness. The design aims to balance resemblance to existing instances with novelty, while retaining properties that matter for solving and learning from the generated problems.

The reported studies show stronger distributional similarity and 100% feasibility on both easy and hard datasets compared with existing techniques. They also demonstrate preservation of key properties, including hardness, and improved downstream task performance. These findings matter because realistic structure and usable optimization labels must work together for synthetic instances to serve as effective training data.
icml-2024-milp-fbgen-lp-milp-instance-ge.tldr: MILP-FBGen generates realistic optimization instances using diffusion and constrained sampling to preserve feasibility, boundedness, and useful problem structure.

paragraphs: Parameterized-action reinforcement learning involves choosing actions together with the parameters that specify them. This paper introduces Dynamics Learning and predictive control with Parameterized Actions, or DLPA, for that setting. Its central approach is to learn how the environment responds to parameterized actions and use that learned dynamics model when planning.

The agent conditions its dynamics model on the parameterized action, then plans using a modified form of Model Predictive Path Integral control. Learning and planning therefore have complementary roles: the model represents predicted environment behavior, while the controller uses predictions to choose actions. This makes the parameterized action structure part of both the predictive model and the planning procedure.

The authors also analyze the value difference between a generated trajectory and an optimal trajectory through Lipschitz continuity. This provides a theoretical account of planning quality in terms of achieved value. On several standard benchmarks, DLPA delivers better sample efficiency and asymptotic performance than the compared state-of-the-art parameterized-action methods, supporting the proposed model-based approach.
icml-2024-model-based-reinforcement-lear.tldr: DLPA learns parameterized-action dynamics and plans with predictive control, improving sample efficiency and final performance on evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Adversarial training perturbs input examples to improve resistance to attacks, but the paper describes a resulting loss in clean accuracy. Sharpness-Aware Minimization, or SAM, instead perturbs model weights to seek flatter regions of the loss landscape and improve generalization. The authors investigate whether this weight-based training method can also produce adversarial robustness.

The study examines a duality between these two forms of perturbation. It provides theoretical and empirical insights into how SAM can implicitly learn more robust features, even though its original purpose is better clean accuracy. This connects the behavior of the optimization method with the kinds of features the trained model acquires.

Comprehensive experiments show that SAM alone can notably improve adversarial robustness without sacrificing clean accuracy in the evaluated settings. The result suggests that SAM may serve as an alternative when clean accuracy has higher priority. That conclusion is a potential use supported by the findings, rather than a claim that SAM universally provides the same defenses as adversarial training.
icml-2024-on-the-duality-between-sharpne.tldr: The paper finds that SAM can improve adversarial robustness through more robust features while preserving clean accuracy in its experiments.

paragraphs: Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, is commonly understood as a compact way to represent weight changes during model adaptation. This paper interprets its lightweight matrices as controllers acting on the original frozen model blocks. That perspective shifts attention toward how a small trainable component can influence the behavior of a much larger fixed system.

The authors analyze the controllability of these modules and establish sufficient conditions for integrating them effectively into downstream controls. These conditions identify circumstances in which the control approach works; they are not presented as necessary requirements for every successful adaptation. The analysis provides a theoretical basis for reconsidering the design of the adaptation modules.

The resulting redesign introduces nonlinear behavior through a parameter-free attention mechanism that lets tokens interact inside the controllers. Across every assessed dataset and rank configuration, the approach outperforms the existing LoRA algorithms without adding parameters. The findings suggest that richer computation within an adapter can improve adaptation even when its trainable parameter count stays fixed.
icml-2024-parameter-efficient-fine-tunin.tldr: Viewing LoRA as a control system motivates parameter-free attention inside adapters, improving performance across the evaluated datasets and ranks.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when the environment is only partly observable, the learner receives hindsight observations, and the objective accounts for risk. It brings these elements into a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process formulation. Accumulated reward is evaluated using an entropic risk measure, so the optimization target incorporates risk sensitivity.

The authors develop an algorithm with a provable efficiency guarantee for this setting and analyze its regret. The stated bound grows with the square root of the number of episodes, alongside factors involving the problem size, horizon, and risk sensitivity. Its risk-related factor includes an exponential dependence on the product of risk magnitude and horizon.

When the model reduces to risk-neutral or fully observable settings, the bound matches or improves existing upper bounds. The proof uses a change of measure and a new analytical device called beta vectors to simplify the derivations. The contribution combines a learning guarantee for this joint setting with mathematical tools intended to support further theoretical reinforcement-learning analysis.
icml-2024-provably-efficient-partially-o.tldr: The paper provides a provably efficient algorithm and regret analysis for risk-sensitive, partially observable reinforcement learning with hindsight observations.

paragraphs: Neural-network training can involve loss functions that are neither convex nor smooth. Stochastic gradient descent with momentum is widely used in that setting, but the classical analysis described in this paper requires at least one of those properties. The work addresses this mismatch between a practical training method and the conditions supporting its familiar theory.

The proposed change is small: multiply each momentum-based update by a random scalar drawn from an exponential distribution. This randomizes the update’s scale while retaining the underlying momentum method. The authors show that the resulting algorithm achieves optimal convergence guarantees for the nonsmooth, nonconvex optimization setting they study.

The guarantee emerges from a broader framework that converts online convex optimization algorithms into nonconvex optimization algorithms. This matters because the result is more than an isolated analysis of one modified optimizer: the conversion framework explains how the method arises. The stated contribution is a convergence result for irregular objectives, connecting a simple algorithmic change to a general theoretical construction.
icml-2024-random-scaling-and-momentum-fo.tldr: Exponentially distributed random scaling gives momentum SGD optimal convergence guarantees in the studied nonsmooth, nonconvex setting.

paragraphs: In-memory computing performs operations directly where data is stored, addressing both computation and data movement. Its analog outputs must be converted back to digital values using analog-to-digital converters. Limited converter precision helps maintain efficiency but introduces substantial output quantization error. RAOQ targets this specific source of error through quantization-aware training.

The method combines two kinds of intervention. A-shift and W-reshape adjust activation and weight statistics to reduce converter-induced error. BitAug then helps models tolerate the quantization that remains. ADC-LoRA, a low-rank approximation technique, reduces the training overhead associated with adaptation. The design therefore addresses both the production of quantization error and the model’s sensitivity to it.

Experiments span neural networks of different sizes, computer vision and natural-language tasks, and multiple bit precisions. The authors report consistently strong performance and state-of-the-art results with practical in-memory computing implementations. The findings show the value of matching model training to the output-precision constraints of the computing hardware.
icml-2024-reshape-and-adapt-for-output-q.tldr: RAOQ adjusts model statistics and trains for quantization tolerance to improve neural-network performance on limited-precision in-memory hardware.

paragraphs: Learning robot manipulation from demonstrations requires both understanding a scene and predicting useful actions. Existing approaches can demand many high-quality trajectories, struggle with new tasks, and execute long-horizon reasoning inefficiently. SAM-E addresses scene understanding and action prediction together in a multi-task imitation-learning architecture for three-dimensional manipulation.

For perception, the method adapts the pretrained Segment Anything model to extract features relevant to the task. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning on robot data helps this visual foundation model understand embodied scenarios. For action prediction, SAM-E uses a multi-channel heatmap that represents an action sequence and allows the sequence to be predicted in a single pass.

This combination connects general visual knowledge with robot-specific adaptation and longer-term action prediction. Across instruction-following tasks, the authors report better performance and higher execution efficiency than the baselines. They also find substantially improved generalization when adapting to new tasks with few examples. The findings support using pretrained perception and sequence imitation as complementary parts of a manipulation policy.
icml-2024-sam-e-leveraging-visual-founda.tldr: SAM-E combines adapted foundation-model perception with single-pass action-sequence prediction to improve robot manipulation and few-shot task adaptation.

paragraphs: This paper considers reinforcement-learning tasks that share transition dynamics but have different reward functions. In this setting, each task’s Q-function can be separated into successor features describing the shared dynamics and a mapping describing task-specific rewards. That separation creates a basis for transferring knowledge between tasks instead of learning each value function independently.

Successor features are combined with generalized policy improvement, or GPI, to reduce the samples needed to find the optimal Q-function. Although this framework has shown promising empirical results, the paper addresses missing theory when deep neural networks learn the successor features. It establishes convergence analysis and generalization guarantees for SF-DQN with GPI.

The analysis shows faster convergence and better generalization than conventional approaches such as deep Q-networks within the studied transfer setting. Numerical experiments on real and synthetic tasks support those conclusions. The shared-dynamics condition is central to the contribution: it makes the reusable part of the value representation applicable across tasks whose rewards differ.
icml-2024-sf-dqn-provable-knowledge-tran.tldr: SF-DQN with generalized policy improvement gains convergence and generalization guarantees for transfer between tasks with shared dynamics and different rewards.

paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects is a demanding target for foundation models because causal inference involves intricate reasoning and numerical precision. This paper introduces Causal Inference with Attention, or CInA, as a step toward models that can handle such tasks across datasets. It learns from multiple unlabeled datasets through a self-supervised procedure.

The method rests on a theoretical primal-dual connection between optimal covariate balancing and self-attention. Covariate balancing provides the causal-estimation side of this connection, while attention supplies a mechanism available in transformer-type architectures. The authors use the relationship to enable zero-shot causal inference through the final layer of a trained model on new tasks with new data.

Experiments show that CInA generalizes to out-of-distribution and real-world datasets, matching or surpassing traditional methods fitted separately to each dataset. These results support transferring learned causal-estimation behavior across datasets. The paper presents this as evidence of potential for causal foundation models, with treatment-effect estimation providing the concrete task on which that potential is demonstrated.
icml-2024-towards-causal-foundation-mode.tldr: CInA connects covariate balancing with self-attention to learn across unlabeled datasets and perform zero-shot treatment-effect estimation.

paragraphs: Certified machine unlearning pairs data removal with theoretical guarantees. Such methods have been extensively studied for convex models, but deep neural networks introduce highly nonconvex objectives that complicate their application. This paper develops techniques for extending certified unlearning methods to that setting, aiming to retain guarantees while making the computation practical.

A central efficiency contribution is an inverse-Hessian approximation. The Hessian captures curvature of the training objective, and the proposed approximation reduces computational cost without compromising the certification guarantees. This addresses an important tension in the approach: a theoretically supported unlearning procedure also needs an efficient way to perform its required calculations.

The paper also expands its certification discussion to training that has not converged and to sequential unlearning requests arriving at different times. Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate the method’s efficacy and the advantages of certified unlearning for deep networks. Together, these contributions extend both the objective types and the training or request situations considered by certified unlearning.
icml-2024-towards-certified-unlearning-f.tldr: The paper extends certified unlearning to deep networks using efficient inverse-Hessian approximation and considers unfinished training and sequential requests.

paragraphs: Training on several input modalities does not ensure that a network will use all of them. It may rely heavily on one stream while neglecting the others, producing unimodal bias. This paper develops a theory using multimodal deep linear networks to explain how architecture, dataset statistics, and initialization influence that behavior.

The authors calculate how long the unimodal learning phase lasts as a function of those factors, including the depth at which modalities are fused. Their analysis shows that fusing streams deeper in the network lengthens this phase. This connects an architectural decision about where information meets to the timing of how different modalities are learned.

A prolonged unimodal phase can cause weaker generalization and permanent unimodal bias in the overparameterized regime. Although the core results concern linear networks, they extend to nonlinear networks in certain settings. The findings identify a possible training pathology of late and intermediate fusion: combining modalities deeper can leave learning dominated by one stream for a long time.
icml-2024-understanding-unimodal-bias-in.tldr: A theory of multimodal linear networks links deeper fusion to longer unimodal learning phases that can impair generalization and become permanent.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specified data from a trained model. Verification methods give data owners a way to check whether a provider has actually carried out that removal. This paper asks whether a dishonest provider can pass such checks while retaining information from the data it claims to have unlearned.

The authors organize current verification strategies into two categories according to the potential dishonesty they address. They then introduce two adversarial unlearning processes capable of circumventing both categories. The central concern is the gap between producing evidence that satisfies a verification procedure and actually removing the information targeted by the request.

Theoretical analysis and experiments on real-world datasets support the effectiveness of these processes. The results expose vulnerabilities in the verification strategies studied and show why a successful check can be misleading under adversarial provider behavior. The contribution is an examination of verification fragility, establishing concrete failure modes that further work on trustworthy unlearning needs to address.
icml-2024-verification-of-machine-unlear.tldr: The paper shows that adversarial unlearning processes can pass existing verification strategies while retaining information supposedly removed.

paragraphs: A watermark places a detectable statistical signal in generated output. Strong watermarking would prevent a computationally bounded attacker from erasing that signal without substantially reducing output quality. This paper proves that such protection is impossible under specified assumptions, including when watermark insertion and detection share a secret key unavailable to the attacker.

The result depends on two capabilities. A quality oracle must judge whether an output remains a good response, and a perturbation oracle must modify outputs with a nontrivial chance of preserving quality. Those modifications must also induce an efficiently mixing random walk over high-quality outputs. Under these conditions, the proposed attack works without knowing either the key or the watermarking scheme.

The authors argue that these capabilities can be practical even for an attacker weaker than the generating model. Their implementation removes watermarks from three existing language-model schemes with only minor quality degradation, and they report preliminary vision-language results. The impossibility claim is conditional on the oracle assumptions, while the experiments demonstrate feasibility for the tested schemes.
icml-2024-watermarks-in-the-sand-impossi.tldr: Under explicit quality and perturbation-oracle assumptions, strong watermarking is impossible even with secret-key detection.
